Entries.Text: Navigation
Navigation Editor
This tool supports Elden Ring, Nightreign, The Duskbloods, Armored Core VI, Dark Souls III, Bloodborne, Sekiro, Demon's Souls, Dark Souls, Dark Souls Remastered and Dark Souls II (including SOTFS).

View, edit, generate and check the navigation data of a loaded map: the navmeshes its characters use for pathfinding, and how they connect. Start in the Overlay tab, which draws the navmesh in the viewport; the editing tabs work on what it draws. A typical workflow for a new navmesh is Models (Generate), then Stitch, then Gates, then Check.

1. Tick Show overlay above the tabs, and choose the n or o set.
2. Turn layers on or off: faces, edges, links and gates. Each line layer shows its colour.
3. The other tabs edit what the overlay draws. To hide the Map Editor's own navmesh drawing, use the Navmesh render filter.

1. Load the map with Havok and collision loading on, and also its neighbours if its NVC files should be joined.
2. Choose the options (the defaults suit a vanilla map: they keep what its navmesh reaches, its models, face data and links), then click Regenerate Map. The n and o settings are the Models tab's Generate settings.
3. When it finishes, review the result with the overlay, then click Validate in the Check tab.
The whole regeneration is one undo step. Saving the map writes the NVA, the navmesh binder and the changed NVC files.

1. Generate: select collision parts or assets in the viewport (with the map's collision loaded), tick Blocker on parts to go around, choose the target, and click Generate.
2. Or Duplicate a model, moved by an offset, or Remove one, which leaves a placeholder.
3. Then click Stitch model to join the new model to its neighbours.
Each edit is one undo step. Saving the map writes the files.

Needs the overlay.
1. Choose the scope: the drawn set, the picked face's navmesh, or the selected model.
2. Find lists the broken connections and the new pairs. Nothing changes yet.
3. Apply makes the changes as one undo step. With Update gates on, it also rebuilds the gates of the changed pairs.
Each set is stitched separately: switch between n and o above the tabs and click Find again.

Needs the overlay.
1. Tick Pick and move gates, then click a face or a gate marker to choose its navmesh.
2. Rebuild its gates after its connections change, or add, remove and drag gates by hand.
3. Recompute its costs after moving its vertices.
Gates join the navmeshes of one map for the game's long-range pathfinding. They never cross maps.

Needs the overlay.
1. Tick Add links, and set Both ways and the edge data (Jump, Fall).
2. Click the face the link starts from, then the face it leads to.
3. Pick a face to see, block or remove its links.
In Dark Souls III, Bloodborne and Sekiro, links are user edge setups instead: a box at the ledge and one where it lands, on any navmesh.

Needs the overlay.
1. Tick Pick and click a face to see its data and edges, and type a new value.
2. Or tick Paint, choose Set, Add bits or Remove bits and a value (the bits, or a legend entry's Use), and drag over faces.
3. Each stroke is one undo step. Face data changes no indices, so connections stay valid.

Needs the overlay.
1. Click Start Navmesh Edit, pick a Brush mode (Raise, Lower, Drag or Smooth) and its Radius, and move the mouse over the drawn navmesh: the sphere shows the brush's reach.
2. Hold the left mouse button to brush. While held, Raise, Lower and Smooth apply again at each interval; Drag slides the vertices under the brush with the mouse.
3. Commit Changes writes the moved vertices as one undo step; Discard Changes restores them. Until then, they stay pending on any tab.
After moving outer edges, stitch again. After large moves, recompute the gate costs.

1. Validate checks the map against the rules the game files follow, then compares the result with the vanilla files in the background.
2. New issues come from the project; inherited issues are also in the vanilla files.
3. Click an issue to go to its navmesh, face or gate.
Validate again after editing. The header shows when the result is out of date.
In game (Elden Ring), the exe has the debug switches Game.Navimesh.DisableNvc and Game.Navimesh.DisableNavimesh. With a tool that opens the debug menu, toggling NVC off and on separates the effect of a cross-map edit from an in-map one.
Glossary
The navigation terms the tabs use.
Navmesh

The surface characters use for pathfinding: faces (polygons) joined by edges. A map's NVA file lists its navmeshes, one entry per model and set. The meshes themselves are Havok files in the map's nvmhktbnd binder.
n and o sets

Most games keep two navmeshes of each model: n for normal characters and o for huge ones (Elden Ring's exe labels it Huge; its clearance reaches 5.1 m, compared with 1.53 m for n). The o set usually has fewer faces. Each set has its own connections and links, and is edited separately. The game identifies the sets by the NameID (prefix 0/1 n, 2/3 o) and by the file's ID in the nvmhktbnd (10000s n, 20000s o), not by the file name. Armored Core VI has only the n set.
NameID

The ID that connections, gates and node banks use for a navmesh. The game gives n entries NameIDs by a rule (based on their position in the list or their model ID, depending on the game). An o entry repeats its n entry's NameID plus a fixed offset (2,000,000,000 in Elden Ring).
Placeholder
A navmesh entry without faces. A free placeholder, with no faces in either set and no gates, can hold a generated or copied model. Removing a model turns it into a placeholder.
Quarters (q files)

Some large Elden Ring navmeshes are split into four q files, and their n file is then empty. The game finds quarter k by the file's ID in the nvmhktbnd (40000 + 1000 × k) and the high byte of the entry's Unk50. Quartered models can't be removed or copied, and a map that has them can't get new models; use a free placeholder there.
The game reads only the 6 model digits after the map part of a navmesh file's name. It doesn't read the map part itself, which is why some _10 tiles use their _00 tile's names.
Connections (connectors, NVC)

Joins between boundary edges of two navmeshes, so a path can cross from one to the other: NVA connectors within a map, and NVC files between neighbouring maps. A boundary edge with no connection is open. The Stitch tab finds and creates them.
Links (user edges)

Jumps, drops and ladders between two faces of one navmesh. Each is a pair of user edges, one on each face; a one-way link has its return edge blocked. The edge data sets the kind: 0x2 jump, 0x4 fall, 0x10 extra cost.
Gate nodes

Points where two navmeshes of a map meet, at most 16 per navmesh, each paired with a gate on the other side. The game's long-range pathfinding goes from gate to gate, using the walking cost stored between each pair of gates in a navmesh.
Clearance
How wide a character can be and still pass, cached per edge and vertex in the navmesh file. Edits recalculate it around what they change.
Face data

A 32-bit value per face that pathfinding reads: impassable, high cost, lava, ladder, gated (opened at runtime, for example by a door), and others. The Face Data tab names the known bits and colours the faces by value.
Node banks
Lists of navmesh faces in the NVA, some with an entity ID. In Elden Ring, EMEVD 2003[13] turns the impassable bit of a bank's faces on or off, to block a path until an event flag is set.

Overlay
What the overlay shows. It is drawn slightly above the navmesh and can't be selected.
Show overlay

Draw the overlay of the map picked above. Reading a map's navmesh files for the first time can take a moment. To hide the Map Editor's own navmesh drawing, use the Navmesh render filter, which doesn't hide the overlay.
n set
The n navmeshes (n files, and the q files they are split into), the first half of the NVA's entries: the ground for normal-sized characters.
o set

The o navmeshes (o files), the second half of the NVA's entries: the same ground as n, for huge characters (Elden Ring's exe labels the set Huge; its clearance values reach 5.1 m, compared with 1.53 m for n). They usually have fewer faces.
Face opacity
How opaque the face fills are.
{0} user edges lead to a face that couldn't be found, so they are drawn without an arc.
Layers
The parts of the overlay to draw, and their colours.
Faces
The faces, filled with a colour for each face data value. The legend below lists the values.
Inner edges
Edges between two faces of the same navmesh. Dense on large maps.
Open edges
Boundary edges that no connection joins to another navmesh.
Connected in the map
Boundary edges that an NVA connector joins to another navmesh in this map.
Connected to a neighbour
Boundary edges that an NVC file joins to a navmesh in a neighbouring map.
User edges
Jump, ladder and drop links: the edge, and an arc to the face it leads to.
Blocked user edges
User edges that also carry the blocked flag.
Gate nodes
The NVA's gate nodes that pair with a gate of their neighbour, as see-through diamond markers. A gate and its partner share one point, so each has a short tick into its own navmesh.
Unpaired gate nodes
Gate nodes without a partner. In the game's files, they all point at a navmesh that already has 16 gates.
Broken gate nodes
Gate nodes whose target navmesh doesn't exist or isn't connected to them, or whose partner doesn't point back.
Gate costs
For the navmesh selected in the Gates tab: a line between each pair of its gates that can reach each other, labelled with the cost in metres.
Runtime cuts

The bounds of loaded assets whose AssetEnvironmentGeometryParam row has a navimeshFlag (Obstacle, Impassable or High Cost), filled in amber. The game cuts or marks the navmesh under them at runtime, and lifts this when the asset breaks. The game's own navmeshes run under these assets, so they don't need to be cut out of a generated one. Only assets the game cuts in the drawn set are shown: navimeshFlagApply Type 0 cuts the n set, Type 1 the o set, and Type 2 both. Drawn for assets whose model is loaded, in every loaded map.
Flying volume

The overall shape of the map's flying navigation volume (the .nvvhktbnd that flying enemies path through), as an outline: its floor and ceiling shells and the box of its grid.
For each patch of the map, the floor is where the air over the terrain (or under a roof) ends going down, and the ceiling is the top of that air. Space inside or under the terrain, and holes inside the shape, aren't shown. The map is split into at most 128 patches per side, so small details are smoothed out.

Remove bits

The value to paint, in hexadecimal. The bits below and the legend's Use buttons also set it. The bits list every bit the game's navmesh code reads, by name, and any other bit the drawn faces use.
A bit that the drawn faces use. Its meaning in game is unknown.
Use
Paint this value.
The face's data in hexadecimal. Changing it is one undo step.
Blocked
The user edge's blocked flag (EDGE_BLOCKED). Changing it is one undo step.

The user edge's data in hexadecimal: 0x2 for a jump, 0x4 for a fall (with the drop in tenths of a metre in the high byte), and 0x10 for an extra cost, e.g. 0x204 or 0x314 in the game files. Changing it is one undo step.
(unknown)
Impassable
No character can cross the face. In Elden Ring, EMEVD 2003[13] adds or removes this bit at runtime on a node bank's faces, by its entity ID, to block a path until an event flag is set.
High cost
Crossing the face costs 100 times as much in pathfinding (not in sealed worlds).
Checked
One of the bits that make the game check a character before it crosses the face. No rule for this bit alone was found.
Lava
Only characters whose NpcThinkParam enables Lava navigation cross it, or characters in a runtime state set by the game, at an extra cost.
Ladder
Only characters whose NpcThinkParam enables Ladder navigation cross it.
Opens 0x10000
Lets characters cross a face with 0x10000. The game files never set it; it is added at runtime with the navmesh's dynamic face flags.
Gated (needs 0x8000)
No character crosses the face unless 0x8000 is also set, which happens at runtime: for a face that something in game opens, such as a door.
Huge enemy area
Costs more, by a world setting, for characters that avoid huge enemies (NpcThinkParam isNoAvoidHugeEnemy off).
Opens 0x100000
Lets characters cross a face with 0x100000. The game files never set it; it is added at runtime with the navmesh's dynamic face flags.
Gated (needs 0x80000)
No character crosses the face unless 0x80000 is also set, which happens at runtime.
High cost
Crossing the face costs 100 times as much in pathfinding, on top of 0x8.
Character limit
Characters cross it only when a value of their physics (probably an angle) isn't above a limit stored in the navmesh. The value hasn't been identified. Only n faces use it.
Jump
A jump link, taken by characters whose NpcThinkParam enableJumpMove (enableJumpMove_onBattle in battle) allows it.
Fall
A drop link, taken by characters whose NpcThinkParam useFall_onNormalCaution (useFall_onSearchBattle in battle) allows it.
Extra cost
The link costs more: 4 for a jump, 2 for a fall.
Links

Add and remove links: jump, ladder and drop links between two faces of the same navmesh. A link is a pair of user edges, one on each face, as in the game's files. Each set (n and o) has its own links.
Add links in the viewport

While on, the first click on the drawn set picks the face a link starts from, and the second click picks the face it leads to and adds the link. This turns off picking and painting, and turns itself off when you leave this tab.
Both ways
Characters can use the link in both directions. When off, the return edge is blocked (EDGE_BLOCKED), as in the game's one-way links such as drops.
The edge data (hex) given to both edges of a new link. The game's links use 2 for a jump, and values ending in 04 or 14 for a fall, with varying higher bits.
Clearance

The clearance cache value of the new edges: how wide a character using the link can be, as a fraction of the cache's ceiling (254 = the ceiling, 1.53 m in the n set and 5.1 m in the o set). The game's links use values such as 69, 102, 135 and 168.

Stitch

Re-stitch the connections of the drawn set: find connections whose edges no longer fit, and boundary edges of two navmeshes that lie along each other, within the map (NVA) and across its NVC files with loaded neighbours. Find shows what would change; Apply makes the changes as one undo step.

Include loaded neighbours
Also join edges across this map's NVC files, with neighbouring maps that are loaded with their navmesh files. Only existing NVC files are used, unless Make missing NVC files is ticked.
Make missing NVC files

Open world tiles only. Also join edges with loaded neighbouring tiles (including diagonals) that have no NVC file with this one, and create the file on Apply, named as the game names it: the smaller map ID first, storing connections from that map to the other. It is saved to map/nvc in the project, and the project's folder scan finds it when the project is reopened.
New NVC files on Apply: {0}.
Only join open edges

Only join edges that have no connection yet, which changes the game's data the least. When off, an edge that already has a connection can get another, as the game's partly overlapping edges do. This repairs more, but also adds pairs that the game left unjoined.
Max separation
The largest horizontal distance (seen from above) between two edges that are joined. Half the game's connections are 0, and 90% are under 2.3 cm.
Max step height
The largest height difference between two joined edges where they overlap. 99% of the game's in-map connections are under 0.46 m.
Min overlap
The minimum length two edges must overlap by to be joined.

The horizontal size of a voxel. Smaller values follow the collision more closely, but take longer.

The vertical size of a voxel. Smaller values place faces closer to the collision's height and separate steps more finely, but use more memory.

How far a simplified boundary can stray from the voxels' outline. Smaller values follow walls and ledges more closely, with more corners; larger values cut corners and keep the mesh further in from where the collision ends.
Min region area
Islands of walkable area smaller than this are dropped: the tops of rocks, crates and props no one can reach. 0 keeps every island.
Merge region area
Regions smaller than this are merged into their neighbours before faces are made, so a floor gives fewer, larger regions. This changes how Recast lays out the faces, not what is covered.
Max corners per face
The maximum corners per Recast face, from 3 to 6. 3 gives only triangles; more gives fewer, larger faces. The face grid and the contour split can cut them further.
Snap to collision

Move each vertex onto the collision surface just below or above it, like the game's navmeshes. When off, vertices stay at the voxels' heights, up to one cell height off the collision, and the contour split isn't made (it needs the collision surface).

The maximum length of a boundary edge. 0 for no limit.

The overall shape of the generated faces. Tiles cuts the mesh along a world grid into even squares. Triangles keeps the shape of the walkable area, like the game's navmeshes: larger triangles across open ground, and smaller ones along edges and bumps.
Tiles
Faces cut along a world grid of the face size: even tiles, the same everywhere.
Triangles
Recast's own triangles, with edges longer than the max triangle edge halved, and thin slivers flipped onto their other diagonal where that gives fatter triangles that still lie on the collision.
Max triangle edge
Max triangle edge: off (Recast's size)

The maximum length of a triangle edge. Longer edges are halved, in both faces that share them, until none is longer. Smaller values give more, smaller triangles; 0 keeps Recast's triangles at their own size, which can be long and thin across open ground. Coverage doesn't change.
Face size: off (Recast's faces)

Split every face along a world grid of this size, so the faces are even (links and face data are set per face), and none is wider than the size along X or Z. The grid lines are at whole multiples of the size, so neighbouring models split their shared borders the same way. 0 keeps Recast's faces, which can be several metres across. Coverage doesn't change.

Spill: off
Simplify the result

Clean up the finished navmesh: collapse short edges and flip sliver triangles onto the other diagonal, leaving fewer, fuller triangles like the game's navmeshes. A change is only made where every face stays within the error below of the collision, no face flips or gets thinner, and the outline (walls, cuts, map borders) keeps its shape. The faces become triangles. On by default for Dark Souls II; off elsewhere, where the face grid evens out face sizes for links and face data.
Simplify error
How far a simplified face can stand off the collision, in metres. Higher values give fewer, larger faces that follow the ground less closely.
Follow the collision
Follow the collision: off

How far a face can stand off the collision under it before it is split, in metres. Generated faces have corners only where their outline turns, so a mound or dip inside one is lost and the face cuts flat through it; the game's navmeshes follow the ground. With this on, faces are split, and their new corners placed on the collision, until no edge midpoint or face centre is further off than this. Lower values follow the ground more closely, with more faces. Off keeps the flat faces.
Starts at 0.15 m for Tiles and 0.4 m for Triangles (which then keeps sizes close to the game's triangles). Changing the face shape sets it to the new shape's value, unless you changed it by hand.

The shortest edge that following the collision creates, in metres. Bumps smaller than this are left as they are.

Let the navmesh extend this far past a ledge of its collision, level with the ledge. Recast keeps the mesh one agent radius in from every edge; the spill moves the boundary vertices at a drop out to the ledge and beyond, so the faces on either side of a jump or fall come close together, as the game's AI needs to use the link (ER, NR). Vertices against a wall, or where the way out meets the collision or a blocker, stay where they are, and blockers still cut the spilled faces. 0 for none.
Triangles only
Split every face into triangles after the grid. A corner on a straight edge shared with a neighbour is kept, so a few faces may have four corners.
Jump and fall links

Add links between faces based on the height change across each ledge and gap. From every boundary edge, about every metre, the first surface outward within reach is linked. Within the jump height either way, it becomes a two-way jump (edge data 0x2); lower, down to the fall height, a one-way fall (0x4, with the drop in tenths of a metre in the high byte, like the game's). No link is made where the path through the air meets collision or a blocker, or where the faces are already a short walk apart.

Jump height: off (falls only)
Ends that differ in height by up to this, either way, are joined by a two-way jump. The game's n jumps are mostly within 2.6 m. 0 makes only falls, like the game's o meshes.
Fall height
The deepest drop a fall link goes down. Drops deeper than the jump height and the climb are one-way falls. The game's falls go down by up to about 15 m.
Link reach
How far out from a ledge or gap to look for the landing, horizontally. The game's links reach up to 5 m in n and 9 m in o.

Regenerate Map
Rebuild the map's whole navigation from its collision and assets: every model's n and o navmesh, the NVA, the connections, gates and node banks, and the NVC files to loaded neighbours. One undo step.

Generate each set once over the map's low collision, placed by its collision parts (including new and edited collision), and every asset's collision (with the n and o settings of the Models tab's Generate group). Keep what is reachable from the map's enemies and players, and split it into one navmesh per collision model, joined to each other exactly. On a vanilla catacomb or cave, this covers 85-92% of the game's navmesh, with 86-98% of it on the game's navmesh. Doors, gates and fog walls are solid in the input, so rooms behind them may be cut off; check the result with the overlay and Validate. Maps with quarter (q) files aren't supported.
